# Rule

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

Where is the line you want to compare every value against? Most marks read two
positions. `rule` reads one and draws a line there, across the whole panel along
the other axis. That line is a **reference line** at a threshold. A short line
drawn in from the edge of the panel is a tick. One tick for each row makes a
**rug**, which shows where the observations are.

Most plotting libraries draw a reference line and a rug with three marks: a
vertical reference line, a horizontal one, and a rug. gog has one. A vertical and
a horizontal reference line differ only in which axis holds the position. gog
finds that axis from the columns, as it does for a [bar](bar.qmd#horizontal-bars).

## A line at a threshold {#a-line-at-a-threshold}

Is a country's life expectancy above 70 or below it? On a scatter the reader has
to find 70 on the axis and judge each point against it. With a line at 70, each
point is compared with the line instead of with the axis.
`gapminder_2007` holds 142 countries in 2007, one row for each. `life_bands`
holds three thresholds, one row each: 60, 70 and 80 years. Here they are as a
scatter of life expectancy against income, with a line at each threshold. The
plots in this chapter turn the gridlines off with `theme(grid = "none")`, so
the reference lines are the only lines across the panel, and
`style(color = "firebrick")` draws them in a color apart from the blue points.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
peek(life_bands)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "firebrick") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Three thresholds, one table") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the
life bands, colored firebrick."*

The sentence names `rule` once, and the plot draws three lines. That is the
mark's most useful property: its position is a *column*, not a number.
`life_bands` holds three values, one per line. Add a fourth row and a fourth
line appears with no change to the plot's sentence at all.

Every channel works this way: `color(band)` names a column, not a color. A
column can hold a different value in each row, so a rule can draw a different
line in each panel of a plot. The `continent_means` table
has two columns, `continent` and `life`: each continent's mean life
expectancy in 2007, computed from `gapminder_2007` and rounded to one decimal.
Split the plot into one panel per continent with `facet(continent)`, and each
panel shows its own continent's line:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(continent_means)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(continent_means) + rule + style(color = "firebrick") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each continent's mean, in its own panel") +
  theme(grid = "none") |
  facet(continent)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the
continent means, colored firebrick, split into panel columns by continent."*

Each panel shows only its own continent's row of `continent_means`: the line is
drawn at 54.8 years in Africa and at 77.6 in Europe. A rule's values are placed
on the axis like any other column's, on a log scale too. In polar the same rule
becomes a ring, as [In polar](#in-polar-the-ring-and-the-spoke) shows.

A rule takes no transform, so it cannot compute a reference for you. [What it
refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows that refusal. Which reference you need decides
which mark you write:

| Mark | The reference it draws |
|---|---|
| `rule` | a line at each value in a column you supply ([A line at a threshold](#a-line-at-a-threshold)) |
| `line * mean` | the mean of each group, joined into a [profile](line.qmd#a-category-on-the-domain-the-profile); drawn here as a radar in [In polar](#in-polar-the-ring-and-the-spoke) |
| `ribbon * bounds` | a band between a low column and a high one ([A pre-computed band](ribbon.qmd#a-pre-computed-band)) |
| `zone * bounds` | a block across the panel, between the same two ([Thickness as data](#thickness-as-data)) |
| `line * straight` | the least-squares line through the points, a sloped reference line ([`straight`: the least-squares line](../transforms.qmd#straight-the-least-squares-line)) |

For a line at the overall mean, compute the mean yourself, put it in a column,
and draw `rule` from the table that holds it. For the 2007 table, that column
holds one value: 67.0, the mean life expectancy in years. A table of one row can
be written inside the sentence:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(data.frame(life = 67.0), name = "life_mean") + rule +
  style(color = "firebrick") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A line at the mean, 67.0 years") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given one row with
life 67: a rule colored firebrick."*

85 of the 142 countries lie above the line and 57 below it, so the mean is
pulled down by the countries with the shortest lives.

A sloped reference line, such as the one R draws with `abline(lm(y ~ x))`, is
not a rule, because its height changes along `x`. In gog it is `line *
straight`, the least-squares line through the points, which [`straight`: the
least-squares line](../transforms.qmd#straight-the-least-squares-line)
explains:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  line * straight + style(color = "firebrick") +
  x_label("GDP per person (log scale)") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A sloped reference line, fitted by line * straight") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, and also a
line derived by straight, colored firebrick."*

The line rises about 16.6 years of life expectancy for each tenfold rise in
income, such as from $1,000 to $10,000. The countries far below it live much
shorter lives than the line gives for their income.

A line with a slope and a point you choose, rather than one fitted to the data,
is drawn from its two end points. Put them in a two-row table whose columns are
the plot's own, and draw it with `line`. The `iris_flowers` table holds 150 iris
flowers, with each one's sepal length and petal length in centimeters. Both are
lengths, so the line y = x, with slope 1 through the point (4, 4), marks where a
petal and its sepal are equally long:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + point + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
  data(data.frame(sepal_length = c(4, 8), petal_length = c(4, 8)),
       name = "same_length") +
  line + style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("Sepal length (cm)") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("y = x, drawn from its two end points") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is petal length; then
given two rows with sepal length 4 and 8 and petal length 4 and 8: a line colored
firebrick, with pattern dashed."*

Every flower lies below the line, so every petal is shorter than its sepal. The
line runs only between its two end points, so choose them near the ends of the
axes. An end point outside the data stretches the axis, which is why the petal
axis here reaches 8. For a slope `b` through the point (`x0`, `y0`), the height
at an end `x1` is `y0 + b * (x1 - x0)`.

## Horizontal or vertical {#horizontal-or-vertical}

Nothing in the read-aloud sentences under the two plots above said "horizontal". The mark
took the direction from the columns instead. `life_bands` has a `life` column
and no `gdp` column, and the plot's `y` is `life`. So only the `y` axis has its
column in the rule's table. The rule marks each value on that axis and spans
the other one.

A threshold on income needs a vertical line, and there is no second mark for it.
Give the rule a table that holds `gdp` instead, and the same word draws the line
vertically. Here the table is one row holding one income, $10,000, written
inside the sentence:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(data.frame(gdp = 10000.0), name = "gdp_threshold") + rule +
    style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same mark, the other axis") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given one row with gdp
10000: a rule colored firebrick, with pattern dashed."*

The table holds `gdp`, the plot's `x`, so the line is vertical.

## A rug of ticks {#a-rug-of-ticks}

A scatter shows where each country is on two axes at once. Another question
asks only how the countries spread along the income axis.
A rug tick reads one position too. It marks one value and extends a short
distance into the panel from its edge. That is a threshold line, only shorter,
and the setting that makes it short is `style(reach = "edge")`:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Where the countries are on the income axis") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules, x is gdp,
with reach edge."*

The rule names `x(gdp)` even though the points already named it. This layer has
no table of its own, so it reads the scatter's, which holds both `gdp` and
`life`. The rule could be placed on either axis, so it has to say which one it
is on.

`style(reach = )` takes one of two words: `panel`, the default, and `edge`. A
tick's length comes from the panel: 3.5 percent of the panel's height, or of
its width for a rug up the side. It is never less than 4 pixels and never more
than 14. The minimum keeps a tick visible in a small facet, and the maximum
keeps it short in a large plot. Every setting except `reach` works as on any
rule.

Look along the bottom. Each tick is one country, drawn at its own income. Below
$5,000 the ticks merge into one solid block: 66 of the 142 countries are in the
first tenth of the income axis. The scatter holds the same countries but spreads
them up the other axis, so the crowding is harder to see.

In general a rug puts the one-dimensional distribution of one column in the
margin of a plot that already shows something else. You read the spread of
`gdp` and still see the scatter, in the same panel.

A second plot can show the same spread. Here a histogram of `gdp`, cut into 30
bins by `bin(30)`, is drawn under the scatter, and the two plots share one
`gdp` axis. [Composition](../composition.qmd) shows how plots are put together
this way.

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("The same incomes, counted below the scatter") +
   theme(grid = "none")) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(gdp) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + theme(height = 150, grid = "none"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, above bars derived by bin
into 30, x is gdp."*

The first bar is the tallest: 40 countries below about $1,900. Together with
the next two bars, up to about $5,200, it holds 66 countries, the same 66 the
rug draws as a solid block of ticks.

### The other axis {#the-other-axis}

The rug so far has been along the bottom, on income. Life expectancy has a
distribution of its own, and overlapping points hide it on the `y` axis too.
A rug is not only for the horizontal axis. The position you name on the layer
decides which axis it is on. Write `y(life)` instead of `x(gdp)` and the
ticks run up the left edge. Write both, as two layers, and the scatter has a
rug along the bottom and another up the left at once:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(gdp)  + style(color = "firebrick", reach = "edge") +
  rule + y(life) + style(color = "firebrick", reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both margins, from two layers") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules, x is gdp,
colored firebrick, with reach edge, and also rules, y is life, colored
firebrick, with reach edge."*

Each rug names one axis, and both read the scatter's table. A single `rule`
layer that names both is refused, because a rule draws one line per row, placed
by one column. The message suggests two layers, one per axis, as [What it
refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows.

The left edge shows a different distribution from the bottom edge. The ticks
are dense above 70, thinnest between 60 and 70, and a little denser again from
60 down to 40. Of the 142 countries, 83 are above 70 and 43 below 60, with only
16 between. This is a distribution with two groups and a thin stretch between
them, not a single group. The bottom rug cannot show this, because its ticks are
placed by income. In the scatter it is harder to see, because the same
countries are spread over two axes.

## Coloring the lines {#coloring-the-lines}

The three threshold lines in the plot under [A line at a
threshold](#a-line-at-a-threshold) are all drawn alike, and nothing says what
each one stands for. Give each line its own color instead, and the
legend prints the band's name beside that color.
A rule draws one line per row of its table, so `color` gives each row its own
color. `life_bands` has a `band` column naming each threshold, and that is the
column to use. The points are light gray and the lines are 3 pixels wide, set
by `style(size = 3)`, twice the default of 1.5, so the three colors are easy to
see against the points:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(band) + style(size = 3) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One line per band, named in the legend") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the
life bands, colored by band, with size 3."*

The legend now says what each line is: Low at 60 years, Middle at 70 and High at
80.

On a rule, `color` takes only a categorical column, such as `band`. That is
gog's choice for this mark; `point` and `line` take a continuous column too. A
continuous column on a rule, as in `color(life)`, is refused:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(life)
```

## Thickening a rule {#thickening-a-rule}

A thin line marks a threshold, but it is not the first thing a reader sees.
Sometimes the thresholds are the reason the plot exists. Then the reader should
find those lines first, before reading the data around them.
`style(size = )` sets a rule's width, and a wide, faint rule reads as a
highlighted band:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.55) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", size = 26, opacity = 0.20) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the
life bands, colored seagreen, with size 26 and opacity 0.20."*

A wide, faint rule is a good way to emphasize a value. Its width is measured in
pixels, not in data. Each wide rule in that plot covers a little over two years
of life expectancy, only because this axis runs from 40 to 80. That does not matter while
the width is only for emphasis. It matters once the width is meant to show a range
of values.

### Thickness as data {#thickness-as-data}

Sometimes the thickness is itself a measurement, not "look here": an area
between two exact values, from one edge of the panel to the other. This is what
a highlight usually needs. The two edges are then data, and the mark whose edges
are positions is [`zone`](zone.qmd). A zone takes a pair of values on one axis
and spans the other, as a rule takes one value and spans the other. Zone has
its own chapter, the next one, which covers it in full. It is introduced here
because it does for a range what a rule does for one value, and a highlight
like this is one of the most common reasons to draw a rule. On the left, a zone shades life expectancy from 60 to 70, with the rules from
`life_bands` on top. On the right, a zone shades incomes below $5,000 and runs
up the panel, with a rule at $5,000. Each one-row table is written inside the
sentence. Up the panel, the two columns are `start` and `end`, written by name,
as [A band up the panel](zone.qmd#a-band-up-the-panel) explains:

```{r}
(data(data.frame(lower = 60, upper = 70), name = "sixties") +
   zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) +
   data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("Across: life from 60 to 70") + theme(grid = "none")) |
  (data(data.frame(start = 0, end = 5000), name = "under_5k") +
     zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
     style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) +
     data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
     data(data.frame(gdp = 5000), name = "at_5k") + rule +
     style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("Up: income below $5,000") + theme(grid = "none"))
```

*"Given one row with lower 60 and upper 70: a zone from lower to upper, colored
seagreen, with opacity 0.18; then given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is
life, and also rules from the life bands, colored seagreen, with pattern dashed;
beside, given one row with start 0 and end 5000: a zone from start to end,
colored seagreen, with opacity 0.18; then given gapminder 2007: points, x is
gdp, y is life; then given one row with gdp 5000: a rule colored seagreen, with
pattern dashed."*

The dashed rules lie exactly on the zones' edges, because both marks read
their positions from data. The edges rescale with the axis and keep the same
values in every facet. Each zone is written *first*, and layers are drawn in the
order they are written, so the points are drawn over it. The left zone holds the
16 countries between 60 and 70, the thin stretch between the two groups in [The
other axis](#the-other-axis). The right zone holds the 66 countries below
$5,000, the solid block of ticks in [A rug of ticks](#a-rug-of-ticks).

## In polar: the ring and the spoke {#in-polar-the-ring-and-the-spoke}

Wind comes from a compass direction, so its speed can be drawn on a circle, as
a radar chart. A target speed on that chart is a threshold like any other. In
polar one of the two axes is bent into a circle. The question is what shape the
line takes then.
The mark does one thing: it draws a line at one position and spans the whole of
the other axis. In polar that is unchanged. A polar plot has two axes, the angle and the radius. A
rule that spans the angle is a ring, and one that spans the radius is a spoke:
a straight line from the center to the rim, the outer edge of the circle. The
[Polar](../polar.qmd) chapter explains how the circle itself is built.

`winds` is a table made for this book, introduced in [The book's
data](../book-data.qmd). Each row is one observation of the wind, with its
compass `direction` and its `speed` in kilometers per hour. `speed_target`
holds one target speed, 15 km/h:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(winds)
peek(speed_target)
```

The angular axis runs all the way around the circle, and one full circle of it
is called the **turn**. A rule that spans the whole turn closes into a ring.
Here it marks a target speed on the radar chart of mean wind speed by
direction, and `speed` is on the radial axis, the one that runs from the center
outward. `limits = c(0, NA)` starts that axis at the center, so a ring's
distance from the center is its speed:

```{r}
data(winds) + line * mean + x(direction) + y(speed, limits = c(0, NA)) + polar() +
  data(speed_target) + rule +
    style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("A target speed, drawn as a ring") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given the winds: a line derived by mean, x is direction, y is speed from 0, in
polar, and also rules from the speed target."*

The dashed ring is drawn at 15. The mean speed is above it at two compass points
only, W at about 21 and SW at about 17. At E it comes close, at about 14.

Without `limits = c(0, NA)`, the radial axis starts at the smallest value the
plot draws. Here is the same plot both ways:

```{r}
(data(winds) + line * mean + x(direction) + y(speed, limits = c(0, NA)) + polar() +
   data(speed_target) + rule +
     style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
   title("Radius from 0") + theme(grid = "none")) |
  (data(winds) + line * mean + x(direction) + y(speed) + polar() +
     data(speed_target) + rule +
       style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
     title("Radius from the smallest mean") + theme(grid = "none"))
```

*"Given the winds: a line derived by mean, x is direction, y is speed from 0, in
polar, and also rules from the speed target; beside the same with y is speed."*

On the right, the center is 8.7 km/h, the mean at S, the lowest of the eight
directions. S is drawn at the center, as if no wind came from the south. W, at
about 21, looks many times stronger than S, though it is about two and a half
times as strong. The ring at 15 is drawn closer to the center and looks smaller. A
reader judges a radar chart by distance from the center, so that distance has
to start at 0.

A rule that spans the whole *radius* draws a spoke. Give the rule a table
holding `direction` instead of `speed`, and the line is drawn at that compass
point. Here it marks W, the direction with the strongest mean wind:

```{r}
data(winds) + line * mean + x(direction) + y(speed, limits = c(0, NA)) + polar() +
  data(data.frame(direction = "W"), name = "west") + rule +
    style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("One compass point, center to rim") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given the winds: a line derived by mean, x is direction, y is speed from 0, in
polar; then given one row with direction W: a rule."*

Neither shape needs anything special in the sentence you write. You write the
ring and the spoke as you write a straight rule, and gog takes the axis from the
column in the rule's table: the ring's table holds `speed`, a radius, and the
spoke's holds `direction`, an angle. In a cube a rule is a plane, and gog
refuses to draw it. [What the cube
blocks](../space.qmd#what-the-cube-blocks) explains why.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists every transform by kind. A rule takes none
of them, so each one is in the Refuses column:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("rule")
```

A rule is placed by one column and spans the whole panel on the other axis. A
transform needs a second
position, to group by or to put its result on, and a rule reads only one. To
draw a value computed from the rows, write a mark that takes the transform:
`line * mean` joins the means of the groups. For a band between a low column
and a high column you already have, write `ribbon * bounds` or `zone * bounds`.
The [line](line.qmd), [ribbon](ribbon.qmd) and [zone](zone.qmd) chapters draw
them. [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows `rule * mean` refused.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

A threshold line has to look different from the data it crosses. Its color and
its pattern can come from a column, as `color(band)` did above, or be set for the
whole layer. Its width and its opacity can only be set: gog gives a rule one of
each for the whole layer, not one per row. Each mark takes its own settings. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are a rule's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("rule")
```

Four of those are a stroke's ordinary controls, and one is the mark's own.
`style(reach = )` sets how far the rule reaches across the panel. The value
`edge` shortens it to a tick. The other four behave here as on `line` or
`path`:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data(data.frame(life = 50.0), name = "at_50") + rule +
    style(color = "firebrick", size = 4) +
  data(data.frame(life = 60.0), name = "at_60") + rule +
    style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  data(data.frame(life = 70.0), name = "at_70") + rule +
    style(color = "steelblue", pattern = "dotted", size = 2.5) +
  data(data.frame(life = 80.0), name = "at_80") + rule +
    style(color = "black", size = 6, opacity = 0.25) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Bottom to top: thick, dashed, dotted, faded") +
  theme(grid = "none")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored lightgray; then
given one row with life 50: a rule colored firebrick, with size 4; then given
one row with life 60: a rule colored seagreen, with pattern dashed; then given
one row with life 70: a rule colored steelblue, with pattern dotted and size
2.5; then given one row with life 80: a rule colored black, with size 6 and
opacity 0.25."*

A rule is a stroke, so `pattern` takes the five **stroke patterns**, `solid`
among them. `style(pattern = "hatch")` is refused, as [What it
refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows.
`"hatch"` is a fill texture, for a filled region. [`bar`](bar.qmd),
[`area`](area.qmd), [`box`](box.qmd) and [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) take it, and so
does [`zone`](zone.qmd), the next chapter.

What a rule refuses follows from the same geometry. There is no `shape`,
because `shape` chooses the symbol a point is drawn with, such as a circle or a
square, and a line is not drawn with one. There is no border either. [What it
refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows both refused.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

The first sentence you are likely to try is a bare `rule` on the plot's own
table. That table holds both position columns, so the rule could be placed on
either axis. Nothing in
the sentence says which axis is meant, so gog refuses rather than choosing one:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + rule
```

That refusal is why every rug in this chapter names its axis, `rule + x(gdp)`
or `rule + y(life)`. A threshold with a table of its own needs no position. That
table holds only one of the two columns, so the axis is taken from it.

One layer that names both positions is refused too. A rule draws
one line per row, placed by one column, so only one of the two columns could be
drawn:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  rule + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(reach = "edge")
```

The message suggests two layers, one per axis. Add `style(reach = "edge")` to
each, and they are the two rugs under [The other axis](#the-other-axis).

A rule takes no transform either. A statistic such as `mean` summarizes one
axis for each value of the other, and a rule reads only one position:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule * mean
```

The message says to compute the value yourself and give the rule a table of the
results, with one row per line. [A line at a
threshold](#a-line-at-a-threshold) does this for each continent's mean.

A rule has no border either. A border is the outline of a filled shape, and a
rule is drawn with a stroke, with no inside to outline:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(border_color = "black")
```

For the same reason a fill texture is refused. `"hatch"` fills a region, and a
rule has none, so the message lists the stroke patterns instead:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(pattern = "hatch")
```

So `style(color = )` is a rule's color and `style(size = )` its width. That is
the same answer `line`, `step` and `path` give, because it is the same
geometry. Mapping a column to `size` or `opacity` is refused as well: a rule
takes one of each for the whole layer.

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + size(life)
```

For a thickness that comes from the data, draw a band with `zone * bounds`, as
[Thickness as data](#thickness-as-data) shows. A rule has no
`shape` either, because a line is not drawn with a symbol:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + shape(band)
```

## In short {#in-short}

A rule's position is a column and never a number, so three thresholds are three
rows. With its column on `x` the line is vertical, and on `y` horizontal.
`style(reach = "edge")` makes it a rug tick, and in polar it is a ring or a
spoke. A rule on the plot's own table must name exactly one axis, or gog
refuses it. It takes no transform, so you compute a mean in a table of its
own.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

A rule marks one value. Its width is measured in pixels rather than in data.
[Zone](zone.qmd) shades a rectangle. With two values on one axis, it is a block
across the panel, the filled form of a rule.
